14.1 OBSERVABLE OPERATIONS
 
INSTRUCTOR NOTES 
 
SAY: 
At Atlas, we aim to embody a safety culture that is proactive, not reactive. 
To do that, we all have to own our culture as we are each leaders setting the tone for every interaction and every flight.

DO: 
Review the mindsets, CRM skillsets, and toolsets content on the slide.
Orient students to the performance standards, handling, SOP, FPM, and CRM. These are the standards of excellence that are expected as a minimum at Atlas.
 
DO: Proceed to the next slide 
 
For task-specific performance statements and standards, reference the Qualification Standards document.

14.1 OBSERVABLE OPERATIONS
 
INSTRUCTOR NOTES 
 
DO: Review the five CRM skills (to the left) that all pilots (PF and PM) will need to apply through every step of the flight, and to effectively mitigate threat (to the right).  
 
SAY: 
TEM is WHAT we do. CRM is HOW we do it.
Let’s review and break down each of our CRM skills.
Communication
Clear & Concise: Keep messages brief and specific during critical phases.
Closed-Loop: Always confirm receipt and understanding.
Verbal & Non-Verbal: Be mindful of tone and body language, especially under stress.
Problem-Solving & Decision-Making
FOR-DEC Model: Use structured processes for decisions.
Collaborative: Include team input to find solutions.
Time Management: Assess urgency and engage resources as needed.
Workload Management
Prioritize: Focus on critical tasks during high-stress moments.
Delegate: Distribute tasks to manage workload efficiently.
Automation: Use automation wisely but intervene manually when needed
Situational Awareness
Monitor Flight Path: Stay aware of aircraft’s position and potential threats.
Anticipate: includes for key changes (e.g., course, altitude).
Focus: Prioritize safety over secondary tasks.
Leadership & Teamwork
Empowerment: Distribute workload and leverage team strengths.
Role Clarity: Ensure PF and PM roles are clear.
Supportive Leadership: Mentor FOs and foster collaboration in decision-making.

ASK: Why do we use CRM?

14.1 OBSERVABLE OPERATIONS
 
INSTRUCTOR NOTES 
 
SAY: 
The Aviate, Navigate, Communicate (and Manage) model of how to prioritize was a helpful model we used based on our manual guidance and usually used during an abnormal or emergency. 
You might even notice that Boeing has a concept in FCTM: FLY, FOCUS, ACT (FCTM: 1.3)
We’ve now adopted the more comprehensive RSO FOR-DEC Model that includes elements of proactive risk mitigation, the elements of aviate, navigate, communicate, but also include the FOR-DEC decision making model and the consideration of time vs no-time. 
Decision-Making can be unstructured without a mental model:
As people, we can be selective, inconsistent,
We have presumptions and preferences,
We hold on to goals too long,
It can follow heuristics rather than analysis,
There’s a gap between theory and experience.
Let’s dig deeper into this model and what it offers us…

Review the Success Criteria for each of the observable behaviors.

SAY:

Anything marked as “Y”, indicates I will need to observe the behavior in order for you to score satisfactory on the event.
Behaviors marked “N’, indicate the behavior is not  necessary to result in a satisfactory event.

DO
Walk through each column on the slide: Simulator Session, Training Method, Grading, and Remediation.
Emphasize that LOE is an evaluation session, not a training session.
Highlight that grading occurs at the event set level, with 8 Phase of Flight event sets and 2–3 Situational Event Sets, each receiving ONE overall grade.
Clarify remediation rules: 25% or more unsatisfactory event sets require remediation.

SAY
The LOE is designed to replicate real-world operations and evaluate technical and CRM skills in a line-oriented environment.
Unlike training sessions, LOE focuses on evaluation. Performance is measured against Qualification Standards.
Grading is at the event set level. Each event set—whether a Phase of Flight or Situational Event Set—receives one overall grade based on performance statements or success criteria, respectively.
